# Lingua — Build Checklist & Progress Tracker

**Purpose:** single source of truth for project state. If Alex steps away for a while, opening this cold should answer "what's done, what's next, where did I leave off" in under a minute. Lives at repo root (`BUILD-CHECKLIST.md`); **CC (Claude Code) commits updates** to it as part of every PR.

**Roles live in `CLAUDE.md` → "Roles — read this first."** Four CC lanes: **Feature CC** (app/engine/UX, draft PRs), **Curriculum CC** (content units, self-merges on green), **QA CC** (tests + reports, builds nothing, never merges), **Idea CC** (ideation — feeds the Feature CC backlog, builds nothing, proposes only). Alex merges everything. Three report/route sections in this doc: **Feature CC backlog** (engine/app work surfaced by other lanes), **QA findings** (bugs/defects surfaced by QA, routed to a lane), and **Idea CC — feature pitches** (ranked proposals for the Feature/Curriculum lanes to pick up).

---

## How to use this doc — READ FIRST

**If you're Alex, resuming after a break:** read **Status at a glance** below, then jump to the first `[ ]` (or `[!]`) item under the current phase. That's your next action. The checked history above it is what's already shipped. Check **Dead ends & gotchas** before retrying anything that "should work" — it may already have failed for a known reason.

**If you're CC, maintaining this doc — marking protocol (follow verbatim):**
This file is updated as part of the PR that completes work. When a task is finished (PR merged to `main`), do ALL of:

1. Change `[ ]` to `[x]`.
2. Append ` — DONE <YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM local>, PR #<n>`.
   Example: `- [x] Add validateContent — DONE 2026-06-21 15:40, PR #11 (CC)`
3. If the work surfaced follow-ups, add them as new `[ ]` items under the correct phase, with a one-line note on *why*.
4. Update the **Status at a glance** block (current phase, last updated, next action).
5. **Never delete** a completed task. The checked list *is* the project memory. Tasks stay in their phase section, checked in place — don't move them to a "done pile."
6. Mark work that's actively being built (PR open, not merged) as `[~]` with ` — STARTED <date>`. Flip to `[x]` only on merge.
7. Use `[!] — BLOCKED ON: <thing>` for anything stuck on a dependency (e.g. Phase 6 is blocked on the Phase 5 backend), so it's never mistaken for a plain todo.
8. When you discover a gotcha that wasn't obvious from the docs — a React 19 / Zustand ordering trap, a CI-vs-local difference, a content-contract subtlety — append it to **Dead ends & gotchas** so the next session doesn't re-walk it. Bugs fixed *within* a feature PR (like the `useSyncExternalStore` ordering fix in PR #11) should also be noted on the parent item so the history is preserved.
9. **Log everything, even concepts (Alex's standing rule, 2026-06-25).** Anything we add, change, or even just discuss as a future idea goes in this file — if it's not actionable now, park it in **Future / come back later** so nothing is lost. Don't rely on memory or chat history; the checklist is the record.

> 📢 **STANDING NOTICE TO EVERY SEAT — THE ACCENT STANDARD (Alex, 2026-09-12; scoped 2026-09-13).**
> **Unit 1, lessons 1–3 teach the accents themselves: hear → speak → type the character.** Not the meaning, not a word containing it — `front: "é"`, not `front: "le bébé"`. Alex: *"teaching accents determines how user succeeds."* **Nothing past u1 l3 changes.**
> ✅ **SHIPPED AND AUTHORED — this notice no longer blocks anyone.** Re-verified against `main` on 2026-09-17 by the de B2 block-1 seat, because "DO NOT AUTHOR IT YET" was still standing here after the work landed, and a stale imperative reads as a live one. **All five languages now carry glyph cards in unit 1** (measured over `src/data/index.js`: fr 8 · pt 9 · es 5 · de 6 · no 5, ids `*-u1l*-glyph*` / `de-u1l*`). Three of the four prerequisites are CLOSED:
> - **(1) the meaning card — CLOSED.** `type: "glyph"` is live (`contract.js` `VALID_ITEM_TYPES`), and `cardRouting.js:574` removes `type:meaning` for glyphs while `:563–564` add `type:produce` and `speak`. A glyph is never asked what it means.
> - **(2) audio — CLOSED 2026-09-13** (clips generated; `pt-u1l1-econj` was the last silent card).
> - **(3) the non-folding typed check — CLOSED, and this is the one that used to invalidate the card.** Measured, not read: `checkProduce("e", { front: "é" })` → **false**, `checkProduce("é", …)` → **true**, `checkReading("è", …)` → **false**. The learner must find the character. Kept dead by a test (`82bd0dc5`).
> - **(4) the keyboard popup — STILL OPEN, and it is the only piece left.** Feature CC, not a content blocker: `TypeCard.jsx` has no accent-hint surface (its only keyboard copy is the Japanese-IME nudge at `:326`/`:345`), so nothing tells a learner *how* to type `é` on their platform. Alex asked for it explicitly; it needs iOS/Android long-press · Windows Alt-code · macOS Option wording.
> **The literal wording fits only 1 of the 15 in-scope lessons (fr l1).** Three crew seats independently converged on the rule that fits all of them: **type the smallest string that cannot be shortened without losing what is being taught** — character (`é`), grapheme (`eau`, `ei`, `kj`), or the minimal word for a *process* (`petit`, `hva`, `vous avez`). The mechanical reason a word works for silence but not for accents: the fold means `bebe` passes for `bébé`, but a silent letter does not fold away.

### 🚨 German B1 merge day — two findings that outrank the band, filed by the crew lead

**1. — ROUTED TO FEATURE CC. THE KONJUNKTIV II LESSON CANNOT BE GRADED. The umlaut IS the lesson and `normalizeReading` folds it away.** Found 2026-09-16 when the three German B1 blocks were first assembled in one tree; `check-collisions --lang de` reports it as a READING collision. Reproduced by calling the grader directly:

```
müsste     learner types "musste"     -> ACCEPTED
dürfte     learner types "durfte"     -> ACCEPTED
bräuchte   learner types "brauchte"   -> ACCEPTED
wüsste     learner types "wusste"     -> ACCEPTED
```

- [ ] **Extend `foldWouldEraseAnswer` from single-character fronts to ANY front whose fold collides with another taught front.** `src/store/answer.js` currently fires it only when the front is one character (the é / ß / ä glyph case). - **Why this one is worse than the accent case:** `de-u38l4` teaches `musste`, `durfte`, `wusste` and `de-u38l3` teaches `brauchte` — the PAST forms — so the learner has already been taught the exact string that now passes the Konjunktiv II card. They are not guessing; they are producing something the course drilled into them, and being told it is right. **`de-u70l3` (block 2, "Konjunktiv II") is currently a lesson that cannot teach the one thing it exists for.** Not a content defect — the cards are correctly authored; the grader is the problem, so per CLAUDE.md it is logged rather than worked around.
- Fifth reading collision, same root, lower stakes: `de-u1l5-schon` (`schön` = beautiful) vs `de-u73l1-schon` (`schon`). Two different words, one fold. Worth keeping both — `schon` is one of the commonest words in German — but the typed-from-audio card cannot tell them apart.

German teaches 9 of the 100 commonest words in the language NOWHERE.** Measured against an external frequency list and verified card-by-card on `main`: **so, nur, sein, da, wird, werden, alles, tun, werde** have zero cards. At the top 300 it is 56 words; top 600, 156.

- **WHY NO CHECK CAUGHT IT, and this is the part worth reading twice.** Across 2,998 German example and drill sentences, `nur` appears **0** times, `so` 0, `alle` 0, `jeder` 0, `wirklich` 0 — while `sehr` appears **472**. Authors write inside whatever the scope checker permits, so "used but never taught" is **0 by construction** and measures nothing at all. A green scope run is evidence about the checker, not about the course. The German B1 block-1 header (`unit51.js` §5) documents the seat contorting sentences around `nur` and `einmal` — `de-u61l1-diegenehmigung` reads "auch nicht einen Tag" because the natural "nicht einmal einen Tag" was blocked. That sentence is the gap made visible.
- **Compounding it, and routed to Feature CC:** `src/data/lint.js` builds its proper-noun whitelist from "capitalised mid-sentence" across all units with no ordering — and German capitalises every noun. Measured: **608 German tokens exempted from the scope check on `main`, 807 in block 2's tree, against 64 fr / 49 pt / 41 es / 12 no.** German's scope lint is ~12× more permissive than any other language's **and it gets weaker as the corpus grows**. Every clean German scope run in this repo, including the crew lead's own, means less than it appears to.

*(RUNBOOK §6 "Block 1's remaining job" step 5, written in advance by the block-1 crew lead. **Do not run it yet** — it is worthless until u63–u87 exist. The lead runs it after folding blocks 2 and 3 in and before merging.)*

> You are a fresh Curriculum CC. Review the **whole German B1 band, u51–u87**, cold — you did not author any of it and you owe none of it the benefit of the doubt. Worktree and branch will be given to you; run everything from there.
> **Do not trust the headers.** Every unit file carries a confident comment block; `src/data/de/unit51.js` calls itself the band constitution. Two of its sections were measurably WRONG on the first pass and were only caught by a gate agent — it claimed "a noun's drill is nominative" (false for 62% of the block's nouns) and "three fronts share a stem with a taught word" (the real number was sixteen). **Check claims against the code and the corpus, never against the prose.**
> **Run these, in this order, and read the output rather than the exit code:**
> 1. `npm run lint:curriculum` · `npm run validate:content` · `npm run test:unit` · `npm run audit` · `npm run build`.
> 2. `node scripts/check-collisions.mjs --lang de` — whole language. LEXEME pairs, MEANING duplicates and READING collisions are all things `validate:content` passes clean. Block 1 found **19 meaning duplicates on a fully green validator**.
> 3. `node scripts/check-drills-de.mjs 51 87` — drills are NOT scope-checked by the lint (`exampleScopeWarnings` reads `example.jp` only), so half of everything authored is invisible to the normal gate.
> 4. `node scripts/scope-strict-de.mjs 51 87` — applies no inflection excuse. Expect ~75 tokens per block of participle/declension noise; what you are hunting is a genuinely untaught word hiding in it.
> **The five questions worth your time:**
> 1. **Does it read as German?** You are the native-speaker proxy; there is no human reviewer. The first pass shipped `den Zug verloren` (German does not lose a train), uncontracted `von dem`/`an dem`, and `es gut meinen` without `mit`. Assume more of that survives.
> 2. **Do the drills teach anything?** Count the frames. Block 1's first pass was 43% “Der X ist sehr ADJ” before it was rewritten to 15%. Check blocks 2 and 3 for the same collapse — it is the natural failure mode of the front-must-appear-verbatim rule.
> 3. **Are the hints TRUE?** There are roughly a thousand etymological and usage claims across the band and nothing validates any of them. Three were wrong in block 1 alone.
> 4. **Is `accept[]` being used as a glossary instead of a grader?** `checkMeaning` grades against `[meaning, ...accept]`, so a “helpful” synonym marks a wrong answer right. `de-u61l4-dasgericht` accepted “dish” on the COURT card until a gate caught it.
> 5. **Did the three blocks duplicate a THEME?** Not just a front — a theme. Spanish B1 hit 159 duplicates across 84 unit pairs that way, and lower-order-wins applied mechanically would have gutted a unit to 6 cards. Compare unit TITLES first, fronts second.
> Report findings by item id with a reproduction. Fix what is unambiguous; file the rest.

> **Your specific hazards, in order of how much they will cost you:**

A finite singular is a SILENT miss — the lint warns, but it is easy to scroll past. Block 1 shipped 288/288 and still had to fix two by hand.
> 2. **DO NOT LET EVERY DRILL BECOME `Der X ist sehr ADJ`.** Block 1's first pass was 43% that one frame and had to rewrite 81 of them. Vary the verb as you write: kommen, liegen, stehen, kosten, dauern, bleiben, wachsen, zeigen, helfen, gelten.

> 4. **CHECK LEXEMES, NOT STRINGS.** German derives relentlessly. Block 1 rejected mögen (möchten is taught and is literally its Konjunktiv), lösen (die Lösung taught), nötig, die Erlaubnis, das Verbot, die Zustimmung, bewirken, überprüfen, die Hilfe, die Reparatur. ## Feature CC backlog (logged by curriculum CC — app/engine lane, not mine to build)

- [ ] **(Feature CC, `scripts/de-vocab-scope.mjs`) THE `// FREE:` SET IS GLOBAL, NOT PER-UNIT — a token freed in u124 is licensed from u1 backwards, so one block can silently cancel another block's scope debt sixty units away.** Filed 2026-09-23 by the German B2 merge seat, after it fired for real. **Mechanism:** `buildScope()` walks every `src/data/de/unit*.js`, matches `/^\/\/\s*FREE:\s*(.+)$/m`, and folds every token it finds into **one corpus-wide `Set`** (`scripts/de-vocab-scope.mjs`, the `FREE` const and the `outOfScope` filter). `outOfScope` then tests `!FREE.has(w)` with **no reference to the declaring unit's order**, while the very next clause — `born.get(w) <= order` — *is* order-aware. So the ordinary taught-word path respects unit order and the FREE escape hatch does not. **Measured on the assembled German corpus: 60 unit files declare a FREE header, 665 tokens between them, 25 of the declaring units are u51+.** **What it actually cost:** German B2 block 3 declared `beim` free in `unit124.js` to cover its own past participles. That un-flagged `de-u61l2-dieverantwortung` (u61) and `de-u76l3-dieurkunde` (u76) — both drills read *"liegt beim"* — two pins on `main`, neither of them block 3's to touch, and the merge seat had to delete them from `ORACLE_FLAGGED` in `tests/unit/drill-scope.test.mjs`. Nothing warned; the pins simply stopped meaning anything. **Why it matters beyond bookkeeping:** FREE is how authors paper over the oracle's morphology gaps, so it is used constantly, and every use is a corpus-wide hole punched in the only vocabulary-scope check German has. It also makes the two bookkeeping styles incomparable — de B2 block 2 left its oracle gaps **visible as 38 flags**, block 3 made its gaps **invisible via FREE and scored 0**, and the 0-vs-144 gap between sibling blocks was read as a rigour difference when it was a house-style difference. **Fix: scope FREE by the declaring unit's order** — record `free: Map<token, order>` instead of `Set<token>`, and license a token only where `freeOrder <= order`, exactly as `born` already works. ⚠️ **Expect pins to move in both directions when this lands**, and correct the list rather than the test. ⚠️ **Pair it with the morphology gap in the item below** — the two are the same underlying problem (`derive()` cannot build a `ge-` past participle, a strong preterite, an inflected adjective, a feminine `-in`, or a preposition+article contraction), and fixing morphology is what would let authors stop reaching for FREE at all. The German B2 merge pinned **38** ids that are purely this gap — `gelten`u58→*gilt* alone is 13 of them.

- [ ] **(Feature CC, `src/data/lint.js`) `lint:curriculum` NEVER READS `drill`, so half of every authored card is invisible to the only scope check a crew actually runs.** Filed 2026-09-22 by the de-B2-block2 drill-fix seat, after finding **106 out-of-scope drills across German B2 u101–u113** that five green gates had all passed. The hole is structural, not a slip: `validate:content` only asserts `drill` is `{jp, en}` with both non-empty; `exampleScopeWarnings` (`src/data/lint.js`) reads **`example.jp` only**; `tests/unit/drill-corpus.test.mjs` asserts a drill BUILDS a card, not that its vocabulary is in scope. The single thing that sees it is `scripts/check-drills-de.mjs`, which is **German-only and has to be remembered**. ⚠️ **And German is one of only two languages that has such a script at all** — verified 2026-09-22: `scripts/check-drills.mjs` hardcodes `no/index.js` + `NO_UNITS` (Norwegian-only) and `scripts/check-drills-de.mjs` is its German twin. **`es`, `fr`, `ja`, `pt` and the four languages just scaffolded (`it`, `nl`, `id`, `ru`) have NO drill vocabulary-scope check of any kind**, so nobody has ever measured their drills. Do not assume the German number is the worst case; it is simply the only one that has been looked at. A drill is cut into `cloze:choice` and `sentence:build` cards, so an untaught word in one is a word the learner is asked to *produce* having never been taught it — the same defect class as an out-of-scope example, in a field nothing checks. **Fix: make `exampleScopeWarnings` read `drill.jp` as well as `example.jp`.** ⚠️ **Expect a large one-off warning jump and do not "fix" it by narrowing the rule** — it is pre-existing debt in every language, previously unmeasured. ⚠️ **And carry over the lesson from the German run: ~26% of what the scope oracle flags is the ORACLE's gap, not a defect.** Of 144 flagged German drills, **38 were forms of words that ARE taught** (`gilt`←gelten, `gedauert`←dauern, `kindern`←das Kind, `betrifft`←betreffen, `solche`←solcher, …) and rewriting them would have churned 38 sound drills. Whoever lands this should improve the morphology table in `scripts/de-vocab-scope.mjs` in the same pass, or the new warnings will be ~1-in-4 noise and crews will learn to scroll past them.

Original text kept below as the record. **(Feature CC, blocks every B2 merge) The PWA precache ceiling is now BELOW the corpus — `npm run build` fails, and content cannot fix it.** `vite.config.js` sets `workbox.maximumFileSizeToCacheInBytes: 4 * 1024 * 1024`; the main chunk is now **4,229,932 B** against that **4,194,304 B** limit — **34.8 KiB over**, not the "2 kB" an earlier version of this line said. That figure was wrong because vite's printed kB is not the byte count workbox checks; a Feature CC reading "2 kB" would shave 2 kB and still be red. Measured on `content/de-b2-block2` 2026-09-17 by building twice: **4,013.73 kB with the 13 B2 units reverted to stubs (green)**, 4,196.44 kB with them (red). So the first B2 block of the first language to land crosses it — and de B2 block 1 is already authored, with block 3 and the whole of no/pt B2 behind it, each block roughly the same 180 kB of index chunk. **Do not raise the constant again**: the comment above it in `vite.config.js` already says so — *"When that lands, split content by language/stage instead of raising this further: precaching an ever-larger single chunk is the wrong end of the trade."* Note `content-es`, `content-fr` and `content-ja` are already separate chunks while **de, no and pt sit in `index-*.js`** — splitting those three the same way is the obvious fix and buys back far more than 2 kB.
- [ ] **(grader) ACCENT TOLERANCE IS ONE-WAY, so the plain-spelled twin of a fold-collision pair still accepts its umlauted partner.** Found by the de A1/A2 frequency retrofit, 2026-09-17, and **PRE-EXISTING — not introduced by it.** GUARD 3 (`tests/unit/corpus-guards.test.mjs`) correctly stops the umlauted card accepting the plain spelling, because `seedItems()` stamps `foldCollides` on the item whose fold differs from its own front. But the PLAIN card never gets that stamp — `normalizeReading("schon") === "schon"`, so the guard's `if (fold === front.toLowerCase()) continue` skips it — and ordinary accent tolerance then accepts the umlauted word as an answer for it. Measured on all four de pairs:
  | pair | umlaut card typed plain | plain card typed umlaut |
  |---|---|---|
  | hatte / hätte | `false` ✓ | **`true` ← leak** |
  | konnte / könnte | `false` ✓ | **`true` ← leak** |
  | wurde / würde | `false` ✓ | **`true` ← leak** |
  | schon / schön | `false` ✓ | **`true` ← leak** |
  So a learner shown "already" can type **schön** and be marked correct, on the exact contrast the pair exists to teach. Three of the four pairs predate this branch; the retrofit added the fourth (`schon`, a top-100 word that previously had **no card at all**). **Routed to Feature CC — it is grader behaviour in `src/store/answer.js` plus a GUARD 3 assertion, not content**, and the fix is to stamp/check both directions of a collision pair, not to remove a card.
- [ ] **`lint:curriculum` matches a drill's front by SUBSTRING while the engine and the unit test use WHOLE WORD, so a drill can pass lint and fail CI.** `src/data/lint.js:392` is `!fold(jp).includes(fold(item.front))`; `tests/unit/drill-corpus.test.mjs` calls `findFrontInExample`, which for a Latin language is `findWholeWord(jp, front)` (`src/store/cardRouting.js:235`, letter-boundary check at `:204`). **Reproduced, not theoretical:** the Norwegian B1 block-2 seat authored `no-u71l4-ulik` with the drill “De to er ulike på mange måter” — `ulike` contains `ulik` as a substring, so lint reported **zero warnings**, and `test:unit` went red on two assertions (`every authored drill routes at least one in-context card`, `every drill contains its own front where the router can find it`). The authoring-time check is the one that is supposed to catch this; instead it green-lights the defect and the failure surfaces a gate later. **Fix:** have `lint.js` import `findFrontInExample` rather than keep its own substring test, so the two agree by construction — the same argument that made `check-lang-scope.mjs` import `normalizeReading`. Logged by the Norwegian B1 block-2 seat, 2026-09-16; confirmed by `fact-checker`.

- [ ] **(engine follow-up) NO LANGUAGE HAS ENOUGH SPECIAL LETTERS TO FILL UNIT 1 LESSONS 1–3 AS GLYPH LESSONS. Not even French.** Raised by a curriculum seat 2026-09-13; the inventory below is counted here from every front in the corpus.
  - **A lesson wants 5–8 cards, so three lessons need 15–24 glyph targets. Distinct special letters actually available:**

    | lang | special letters | enough for 3 lessons? |
    |---|---|---|
    | 🇫🇷 fr | **12** — à â ç è é ê î ï ô ù û œ | ❌ (needs 15 minimum) |
    | 🇵🇹 pt | **11** — à á â ã ç é ê í ó ô ú | ❌ |
    | 🇪🇸 es | **7** — á é í ñ ó ú ü | ❌ barely one lesson |
    | 🇩🇪 de | **4** — ä ö ü ß | ❌ under one lesson |
    | 🇳🇴 no | **4** — å æ é ø | ❌ under one lesson |
  - **Even French is short**, and French is the language the standard was written against. German and Norwegian have **four letters each** — less than a single lesson. Adding multigraphs as targets (`eau`, `ei`, `kj`, `sch`, `ão`, `lh`) helps and is right on its own merits, but de still lands near 9 against a floor of 15.
  - ⚠️ **NOTHING WILL STOP A CREW SHIPPING A 3-CARD LESSON.** `src/data/lint.js:437` errors **only on ZERO** cards; 1–4 is `w(...)`, a warning, in a corpus that already emits **2,999** of them. So a seat authors `no-u1l1` as three cards, the gate is green, and nobody sees red. **Verified in the file.**
  - **Three options, and it wants deciding CENTRALLY** — the failure mode is five crews inventing five different shapes for the same lesson and the constitution being written from whichever landed first:
    - **(a) Let accent lessons run 2–4 cards** and exempt them from the density rule. Honest — Norwegian really does only have three extra letters — but it breaks the 24-card unit shape every other unit holds.
    - **(b) Glyph + minimal exemplar** *(the seat's preference, and mine)*: teach `ø` as a glyph card, then `ei øy` as an ordinary vocab card in the same lesson. Fills six, keeps hear/speak/type on the glyph itself, and the exemplar is where the learner meets it in a real word. Satisfies Alex's *"find it on their keyboard"* for the glyph without pretending there are six of them.
    - **(c) Merge the short lessons** — no l1+l3 become one six-card "letters and combinations" lesson. Cleanest card math, but it changes lesson ids and **wipes mastery**, and costs a lesson slot per language.
  - **Whichever wins, `lint.js` should get a rule that makes the shape enforceable**, or option (a) is what happens by default whether or not anyone chose it.

- [ ] **(Web-Claude / Alex — a BLUEPRINT change) Every language reinvents its own authoring conventions, because the blueprint never asks for them. This is the root cause behind several recent content BLOCKs.** Raised 2026-09-13 by a curriculum seat; **every number below independently verified here against the files.**
  - **`src/data/no/unit1.js` is a 259-line constitution** — 8 numbered binding sections (noun front + gender, verb headword, the `reading` fold, V2 word order, the `example.jp` naming trap, the FREE list + scope rule, fixed greeting formulas, and deliberate A1 simplifications to revisit at A2).
  - **What makes it a standard rather than notes, and the part worth copying: it corrects itself and it delegates judgement.** §1 names its own superseded rule — *"an earlier version of this said 'anything countable takes en/ei/et, no third option', and that is false"* — and then hands the call back to the author: *"Decide by the sense you are teaching, say which sense in the hint, and do not expect the rule to decide for you."* That is what makes it usable as a **cross-crew contract**: a seat can cite §1 to prove another seat's note is a *defect* rather than an *opinion*, which is exactly how the `retning` false "masculine only" note was settled.
  - **Nobody else has one. Measured 2026-09-13 (header comment lines in `unit1.js`):**

    | lang | header lines | FREE list | noun/gender rule | verb headword | fold rule | scope rule |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | 🇳🇴 no | **259** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
    | 🇵🇹 pt | 114 | ❌ | ✅ | partial | ✅ | ✅ |
    | 🇩🇪 de | 65 | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **❌** |
    | 🇪🇸 es | 65 | ✅ | ❌ | partial | ✅ | ✅ |
    | 🇫🇷 fr | 18 | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
    | 🇯🇵 **ja** | **0** | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
  - ⚠️ **Japanese has NO header at all — and `BUILD-BRIEF-language-blueprint.md` calls Japanese "the model" that every language copies.** So a crew told to follow the model finds nothing to follow and invents its own conventions. That is the defect in one line.
  - **It is already costing real rework, not hypothetically:** German u45–50 shipped with **no scope rule in its constitution** and five headers falsely claiming scope compliance; **pt has no FREE list**, which is why its example-scope sweep could not separate legitimate cognates from genuine gaps.
  - **Confirmed by grep:** `BUILD-BRIEF-language-blueprint.md` contains **zero** occurrences of "constitution", "FREE list" or "headword". The §1–§8 shape exists nowhere as a requirement.
  - **The fix:** write the §1–§8 shape into the blueprint as a **required deliverable of the scaffold/block-1 seat**, then backfill fr and ja. The curriculum seat that raised it has offered to draft it and has the working example — **but `BUILD-BRIEF-*.md` is Web-Claude/Alex's in the docs map, so the seat correctly refused to edit it unilaterally.** Needs Alex's word on the direction; the drafting itself is cheap and reversible.

- [ ] **(Feature CC) The accent fold accepts the WRONG WORD on 22 front pairs — my fix of 2026-09-13 caught only 2 of them.** Found by two crew seats reviewing that fix (block 1/pt-B1 and block 3/Norwegian), both independently, both right. `foldWouldEraseAnswer()` gates on the front being a **single character**, and that is the wrong test.
  - **What the fold does:** `normalizeReading` strips diacritics for every non-`ja` language, so two items whose fronts differ only by an accent fold to the same string and **each card accepts the other's answer**. Measured across the corpus 2026-09-13 — **22 pairs**:

    | lang | pairs | the ones that matter |
    |---|---|---|
    | **es** | **12** | `hablo`/`habló` and `trabajo`/`trabajó` — **present vs preterite**, "I speak" vs "he spoke" · `sí`/`si` (yes / if) · `tú`/`tu` (you / your) · `qué`/`que` · `dónde`/`donde` |
    | pt | 5 | `porquê`/`porque` — **same unit, same LESSON (u29l1), and their `reading` is already the identical string `porque`**, so both the typed and reading paths accept either · `às`/`as` · `nós`/`nos` · `a manhã`/`amanhã` |
    | fr | 4 | `là`/`la` · `où`/`ou` · `sur`/`sûr` · `sale`/`salé` |
    | de | 1 | `Sie`/`sie` — ⚠️ **CASE, not a diacritic** (formal vs informal "you"). My fix case-folds deliberately (`É` must pass for `é`), so this one needs a different rule again. |
  - ⚠️ **And it misses the glyph targets it was written for.** `ã` is protected (one character); **`ão` and `ãe` are not** — typing `ao` passes. Those are the literal titled targets of pt u1 l2, *"Through the nose: ão, ã, ãe"*. The one lesson whose entire subject is that diacritic does not require it.
  - **The fix is two rules, not a longer length limit** (both seats converged on this, and widening the length test is explicitly the WRONG move — it would kill the deliberate `cafe` → `café` tolerance):
    1. **Ambiguity:** require the exact front when another item in the same language folds to the same string. Catches all 22. Computable from the front map `contract.js` already builds for uniqueness. Leaves `café` alone, because nothing else folds to `cafe`.
    2. **Glyph type:** require the exact front for any `glyph` item, at any length — the front IS the thing being taught. Catches `ão`, `ãe` and every multigraph the five crews are about to author (`eau`, `kj`, `skj`, `sch`). This rides along with the `kana` → `glyph` generalisation Alex greenlit 2026-09-13.
  - ⚠️ **ARCHITECTURE CONSTRAINT — do not import the corpus into `answer.js`.** `contract.js` imports `normalizeReading` from it, and `data/index.js` imports `contract.js`, so `answer.js` → corpus is a **cycle**. The ambiguity set has to reach the checker as data: either stamped onto the item at seed time (`seedItems()` already stamps `lang`) or emitted as a generated manifest the way `audioManifest.js` is. Stamping is the cheaper of the two and has no staleness failure mode.
  - **Blast radius today:** these are shipped cards in live content, marking wrong answers right. `hablo`/`habló` is the worst — a learner can answer the past-tense card in the present tense and be told they are correct.
Single place for the feature/engine work that's surfaced. Curriculum CC adds here; **feature CC builds.** Detail/rationale for each is in the status block above and the linked briefs.

Counts over u51–u87: **`por isso` 103 · `ninguém` 90 · `no entanto` 49 · `e daí que` 28**, and in u77–u87 alone **32 of 264 examples** use the same `A/O <noun> do/da <noun> é/foi` possessive frame. Fix pattern that worked in B1: give the higher-order card a parenthetical sense — `normalizeMeaning()` strips parentheticals before grading, so the bare gloss still passes, while `senseKey()` in `distractors.js` preserves them, which turns the pair into a legitimate contrast instead of a suppressed distractor.

Hints routinely say "you already met this at u29" or "built on o remédio (u25)", and **nothing in the toolchain verifies those citations** — `validate:content` checks structure, `lint:curriculum` checks vocabulary scope, neither reads a hint. In that one block the gate found: `dever` cited to u37 (taught nowhere in pt; u37 has `devia`), `segundo` cited to u14 (not in the corpus at all), `a tarefa` cited to u30 (u30's TITLE carries the word, no card does), `lembrar` cited to u36 (it is u29), `o remédio` cited to u25 (it is u11), `até` cited to u20 (only `até logo`, u2), `a discussão` cited to u24 (only the verb `discutir` is carded). A wrong citation teaches the learner to look for something that is not there, and it is the kind of error an author cannot catch by re-reading their own work — every one came from writing the unit number from memory. **The check is cheap and already exists:** the pt B1 block-3 seat wrote a script that folds every front in the language, maps it to its owning unit, and prints the corpus fact beside each `(uNN)` citation in a hint; it cleared 7 citations in 264 hints on its own block. Fix direction: fold that into `lint:curriculum` as a warning class (regex the hint for `u\d+` / `(Unit N)`, resolve the named unit, assert the hint's quoted front is actually carded there), or ship it as a standalone `npm run check:citations`. Applies to every language — ja, es and fr hints all carry the same unverified citations.

- [ ] **`normalizeReading` does not fold `ø`, and it silently strips answer tolerance from every Norwegian card containing one (logged by no block 1, 2026-09-03 — DID NOT LAND BEFORE no BLOCK 2 — NOW 29 CARDS).** `src/store/answer.js:47` special-cases `æ→ae` and `œ→oe` by explicit replace, then runs NFD. `ø` has no decomposition and no special case, so `normalizeReading("brød")` returns `"brød"` and fails the contract's `[a-z]+`. Norwegian content works around this by hand-writing those readings ø→o (`et brød` → `etbrod`), which validates — but it kills the fold branch of `checkReading` for exactly those cards, leaving only the literal-string branch. **Measured on the 12 ø cards in no block 1:**
```
FRONT "et brød" (reading "etbrod")      FRONT "en bil" (reading "enbil")
  "et brød"  PASS                         "en bil"  PASS
  "Et brød"  FAIL  <- capital            "En bil"  PASS
  "etbrød"   FAIL  <- no space           "enbil"   PASS
  "et brod"  PASS  <- the MISSPELLING passes while the correct
                      spelling with a sentence-initial capital does not
```
So a ø card loses case- and space-tolerance that all 156 other cards get free. **Fix: add `.replace(/ø/g, "o")` beside the `æ` replace in the non-`ja` branch.** Verified safe: `ø` appears in **zero** es/fr readings, so the blast radius is Norwegian only — and there is direct precedent, since that same function had ligature/accent folding ADDED when French needed it. After the fix the hand-written readings become correct-by-coincidence rather than load-bearing, so nothing has to be re-authored. Not fixed here: engine lane, and the block brief was content-only (RUNBOOK §7).

  **UPDATED 2026-09-03, after no block 2 handed back — the ticket is bigger than first filed, on two counts.**
  **(a) It affects `type:produce`, not just `type:reading`.** Block 2's fact-checker found this and it is verified here: `checkProduce` (answer.js:134) falls through to `normalizeReading(input) === normalizeReading(item.reading)` whenever `produceAllowsRomaji(item)` is true, and that returns true for **any** non-`ja` language (answer.js:124). So the dead fold branch degrades the PRODUCTION card as well. Measured on `et brød`:
```
checkProduce("et brød") true    checkProduce("Et brød") FALSE
checkProduce("etbrod")  true    checkProduce("etbrød")  FALSE
checkProduce("et brod") true  <- the misspelling again
```
  **(b) The card count is now 29, not 12** — block 1 has 12 ø fronts and block 2 has **17**, exactly as predicted when this was filed. Block 3 (u15–20) is still authoring, so the number is not final. The original filing said this SHOULD land before block 2; it did not, and block 2 shipped its 17 with the defect rather than inventing a workaround, which was the right call — the content is correct and the fix makes every hand-folded reading correct-by-coincidence, so nothing needs re-authoring whenever it lands. **One line still fixes all 29+.**

- [ ] **`LATIN_LANGS` omits `no`, so `conjFormsFor("no")` returns the JAPANESE form set (logged by no block 1, 2026-09-03 — blocks no u13).** `src/store/conjugate-latin.js:248` derives `LATIN_LANGS` from `ENGINES`, which holds only `es` and `fr`. Ran it: `conjFormsFor("no")` returns `['dict','nai','ta','te','tara'…]` and `verbGroupsFor("no")` returns `godan/ichidan/irregular`. Harmless today because no `no` unit authors a conjugate card — but **`no-u13` is "Grammar 2 — verbs and particles" and belongs to block 2**, so the first seat to try one will be told to tag Norwegian verbs with Japanese forms. Norwegian needs a `no` engine (its present is beautifully regular — infinitive + `-r` for every person, so the engine is nearly trivial) or an explicit refusal. Related: Norwegian headwords verbs as `å snakke`, and `conjugate-latin.js` documents `front` as the bare INFINITIVE, so whatever lands will need to strip the `å ` marker.

- [ ] **`scripts/check-lang-scope.mjs` cannot be used on Norwegian — its fold disagrees with the engine's, and it has no morphology (logged by no block 1, 2026-09-03).** Two separate defects. **(1) The fold is wrong.** Line 73 is `foldAccents = s => s.normalize("NFD").replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g,"")` — NFD only. `normalizeReading()` in `src/store/answer.js` additionally maps `æ→ae` and `œ→oe`, and neither handles `ø`, which has no decomposition. So the checker "expects" readings like `avære`, `eiøy` and `etkjøkken` — strings containing non-ASCII, which **`validate:content` rejects** under contract rule 9 (`[a-z]+` after normalization). Following the checker breaks a real gate, so all 6 of its reading complaints on `no` were dismissed. Fix: import `normalizeReading` from the engine instead of re-implementing the fold, and give `ø` an explicit `→o` mapping there or accept a hand-written reading. **(2) No morphology, so it flags every inflection.** Norwegian headwords verbs in the infinitive (`å være`, `å ha`, `å gå`) and nouns in the indefinite (`ei klokke`); the present (`er`, `har`, `går`) and the definite (`klokka`) then read as untaught. That is the same documented false-positive class es/fr already live with in `lint:curriculum`, which is why lint reports it as a *warning* — but this script reports it as a `✗ problem` and exits non-zero, so it reads as a failure. All 24 of its scope hits on `no` were verified by hand and every one is an inflection of a taught headword or a declared FREE cognate. Suggest it either match `lint:curriculum`'s warning severity, or grow a per-language suffix table. Not fixed here — RUNBOOK §7: never edit the rule from an authoring seat.
- [ ] **(Feature CC) `normalizeReading` does not fold ø, which kills the fold branch of `checkReading` for every Norwegian ø card.** Filed by no block 1, re-confirmed and measured by block 3. `å→a` folds via NFD and `æ→ae` via an explicit replace at [answer.js:47](src/store/answer.js#L47); **ø has neither a decomposition nor a special case**, so `normalizeReading("a prøve")` returns a string still containing ø and never equals the hand-folded reading `aprove`. Measured on the 10 ø cards in block 3 (13 before u17 was re-authored): `å prøve`, `å prove` and `aprove` all pass, but **`Å prøve` with a capital FAILS**, where every non-ø card accepts all four. Content is authored to be a no-op when this lands — all Norwegian readings are already hand-folded ø→o. **Fix is one line**: add `.replace(/ø/g, "o")` beside the æ replace. Verified safe: ø appears in zero es/fr readings, so the blast radius is Norwegian only, and the same function already had ligature folding added for French.

Block 1 teaches `du` (u2, "you") and `deg` (u1l4, "you") — a learner shown "you" and asked to type it in Norwegian has a 50% chance whatever they know. The fix here is the same shape and costs nothing: gloss `deg` as "you (object)" — which its own `accept[]` already carries — leaving `du` as "you". `meaning` is not an id, so no mastery resets. Block 1's six, enumerated and confirmed by the fact-checker against `content/no-a1-block1`: `no-u7l1-enbat` "En båt er på en sjø." · `no-u7l1-pa` "En kopp er på et bord." · `no-u7l2-ettorg` "Et torg er i en by." · `no-u7l3-hoyre` "Ei kirke er til høyre." · `no-u7l3-venstre` "En kino er til venstre." · `no-u7l3-naer` "En butikk er nær et torg." - [ ] **`check-lang-scope.mjs`: a multi-word front licenses each of its words separately, which hides real teach-before-use.** Surfaced 2026-08-14 closing the `está` seam. The checker splits every front on whitespace and records each word as taught at that unit (`taught.set(w, u.order)`) — deliberate, so `la casa` licenses both `la` and `casa`. But it also means unit 8's **fixed weather chunk `está nublado` licenses the bare copula `está` from unit 8 onward**, and `está` is not actually taught until unit 12 lesson 4. Consequence: the checker reported only unit 7's 10 uses, while **25 further uses in units 8–11 were invisible to it** — the same defect, one unit later, silently licensed. Those 25 are now the only Spanish teach-before-use the tool cannot see. Fix direction: only license a component word when it is a function word or when the front is article + noun (the case the split exists for), not when the front is a lexical phrase like `está nublado`, `hace calor`, `tengo frío`, `me duele`. Spanish alone has ten such chunk fronts, so this will under-report on every language that teaches phrases. Content follow-up is separate and belongs to whoever owns u8–u11 next.

  1. **`pruneStartedLanguages` could not survive its own success.** It inferred "this save carries the retired ja→es→fr cascade seeding" from *a listed language having no content* — sound reasoning (`startLanguage` is content-gated) with a fuse on it, because it only holds while some cascade language is unauthored. French shipping burned half of it; Spanish shipping burned the rest. With ja/es/fr all live the test is false for the very profile it exists to catch, so **nothing was pruned and a pre-language-choice save silently gained two started languages, bypassing `canAddLanguage`** — the same defect fixed on 2026-07-31, back by decay rather than by edit. The signal is now **recorded, not derived**: `startLanguage` stamps `profile.languagesChosen`, a recorded choice is never second-guessed, and pre-flag saves are matched against the cascade's *exact* shape (`["ja","es","fr"]`, in order) then **stamped with the verdict, so any save is classified at most once**. No persist bump and no migration — the flag is additive; `hydrateFromCloud` now carries it across a pull so an older device's blob can't erase it and walk the profile back into the bug.
  ⚠️ **The fingerprint is NOT collision-free, and an earlier draft of this entry wrongly called the design "non-destructive by construction."** A pre-flag save from a learner who genuinely started those three languages in that order is *indistinguishable* from the seeding, because the distinguishing fact was never recorded — so in that one case a deliberately-started, untouched, non-active language is dropped and must be re-added. That cost is now **pinned by a test named ACCEPTED LOSS** rather than left to be discovered. It is the cheaper of the two errors (the alternative is silently acquiring two unchosen languages, bypassing `canAddLanguage`), but it is a trade-off, not a guarantee. Caught by the truth-agent.

The `kept` filter still does — so a *recorded* choice is now exempt from it entirely, because otherwise holding `es` back (a live possibility given the red merge below) would silently delete Spanish from every profile that started it.
  **Browser evidence, stated precisely:** on a tree with all 20 Spanish units merged, two cases were checked end-to-end — a stale `["ja","es","fr"]` save boots to `["ja"]`, and a learner who chose Spanish keeps `["es"]`. Both are cases that *should* succeed; the risky case above is undecidable by construction and was not browser-checked. The throwaway branch was deleted, so no artifact of that run survives in the repo.
  2. **Two more surfaces leaked the ASCII fold, and one of them was the loud one.** `db5e45c` gated Teach/Speak/Trace on `readingIsInformative` — from memory, not from a list — and missed both the Ladder word-bank row (`Ladder.jsx`, 12px grey) and **`GlyphDetail.jsx:78`, the modal that row opens on tap, which printed the fold at 22px bold accent with *no gate at all*, not even `showRomaji`.** Fixing only the row would have moved the leak, not closed it. Both now use the same helper. **The method that missed them twice was not running `grep -rn "\.reading}" src/`, which returns the complete five-surface list in one line** — that grep is the actual lesson, and it's how the truth-agent found GlyphDetail after the fact-checker had already found Ladder. This is live for **French A1 today** (566 items), not just for unshipped Spanish. ⚠️ **Honest limit:** both fixes are by inspection plus the helper's unit tests — I could never get the word bank to render a Spanish word in a scripted browser run (even at rung 3), so neither leak was reproduced live.
  3. **`npm run audit` was Japanese-only *and* could not fail.** It hardcoded `src/data/ja`, so it was a **no-op for every other language while printing "ISSUES: none"** — and `RUNBOOK` §5 sells it as one of five gates. It now walks every language directory, takes a filter (`npm run audit -- es`), reports per-language totals, and keeps id-uniqueness global. Two exit-code holes closed at the same time, both instances of the same reassuring-green failure: **findings now set a non-zero exit** (it previously printed duplicates and issues and still exited 0, so it could never actually fail the gate), and **a bad filter argument is a hard error** (`npm run audit -- spanish` used to be dropped by the 2-letter regex and silently audit *everything* while printing a confident language list). All four exit paths verified, including against an injected duplicate id. It immediately picked up **566 French items it had never once opened**.
- [!] **🔴 MERGE DAY — Spanish is RED combined: 33 validation errors, and the fix is a judgement call, not a dedupe.** Measured 2026-08-05 by dry-merging all three es blocks onto the fix branch. Each block is green alone; together `validate:content` fails with **33 duplicate-front errors** (66 in `lint:curriculum`) — precisely the failure mode the merge seat exists to catch. Breakdown: **block 3 re-teaches 23 of block 1's words**, **block 2 re-teaches 7**, **block 3 re-teaches 3 of block 2's**. In git only `BUILD-CHECKLIST.md` conflicted; the content directories never collided, exactly as the runbook predicts.
  **Do not resolve this mechanically.** "Lower slot number wins" would delete block 3's copies, but the collisions split into two kinds that deserve opposite answers:
  - **Block 2's 7** (`el museo`, `el coche`, `el cielo`, `el año`, `el ojo`, `el día`, `hoy`) are true duplicates. Block 1's sounds unit legitimately owns them; block 2 should use them in examples and drop its cards. Lower-slot-wins is right here.
  - **Block 3's 23 are mostly function words** — `es`, `hay`, `de`, `en`, `con`, `un`, `una`, `son`, `yo`, `tú`, `mi`, `mis`, `pero`, `también`, `menos`, `siempre`. Block 1 picked these up *incidentally*, to build a sounds unit out of real words; block 3's `u12 Grammar 1 — basic sentence` and `u13`/`u14` exist **specifically to teach them**. Applying lower-slot-wins here deletes the grammar units' actual subject matter and leaves the systematic treatment nowhere. The pedagogically right move is for **block 1 to cede the function words to block 3**, keeping only the content words its sound demos need.
  **This is the pilot's headline finding.** Word ownership by slot number optimises for the wrong thing when an early unit *uses* a function word that a later grammar unit is built to *teach*. `RUNBOOK` §4/§7 should say so — "lower slot wins **for content words**; a function word belongs to the unit that teaches it, not the one that first uses it" — before the next language repeats it at scale. Related process hole: block 1's hand-forward note listing its consumed anchors was written *after* blocks 2 and 3 had already authored, so it never reached them. That note has to live on the **scaffold branch before the crews start**, not on block 1's branch afterwards.
  **Why this is escalated rather than fixed:** because **merge day belongs to the merge seat** (`RUNBOOK` §6 step 2 assigns "fix in the merged tree" there, and §0 says merge seats run one at a time), and this needs Alex's ruling on ownership first. An earlier draft justified the deferral as "it spans two other seats' content" — **that was wrong and the truth-agent called it**: the resolution I actually recommend (block 1 cedes its function words) lives entirely in `src/data/es/unit1..6` on `content/es-a1-block1`, which is my own block, my own lane. Only block 2's seven duplicates sit in someone else's files. The honest ground is "I'm not the merge seat", not "they're not my files".

## Idea CC — feature pitches (logged by Idea CC — the ideation lane: proposes, builds nothing)

**Who/what:** Idea CC scans the learning-science + ND-UX space and the current app, and files **ranked, concrete, ready-to-build proposals** here for the Feature (or Curriculum) lane to pick up. Every pitch is mission-aligned (deep understanding over memorization, mechanics over dopamine, ND-first) and grounded in real file refs. Idea CC **builds nothing** — a pitch becomes work only when a lane picks it up and Alex greenlights it; big greenlit pitches get expanded into a `BUILD-BRIEF-*.md`. See CLAUDE.md → "Roles."

*Ranking key:* **[R#]** = impact-per-effort rank within the batch (R1 = do first). Lane tag on every item. Nothing here is committed until Alex says go.

### Batch 2 — sentence & grammar card tier (2026-07-05 brainstorm; Alex's sentence-builder + Idea CC)

**Why now:** the word-level roster is SATURATED (see roster update above). Every card tests a word or a word-in-a-sentence (cloze); **nothing tests the *sentence* itself or a *grammar transformation*.** That's the next tier — where the grammar units (U19–21: copula, particles, ～ます/ました, い/な-adj conjugation) finally get *active production* instead of recognition. Alex's "sentence builder" is the flagship.

**🔑 Shared keystone — a JA sentence tokenizer.** R11/R12 (and optionally R10) all need to split a space-less kana/kanji example sentence into **word + particle tokens**. Feasible via **greedy longest-match over the known-vocab fronts + the closed particle set** (examples are short, space-less, and built only from globally-unique already-taught fronts — the vocab-front uniqueness validator guarantees it). When a sentence won't tokenize cleanly, the card simply isn't offered (safe degradation, exactly like `canCloze`). **Build the tokenizer once → three cards ride it.** Recommend one combined brief: **tokenizer + sentence builder (R11)**, then R10/R12 fall out cheaply.

- [ ] **[R10] (Feature CC — cheapest, highest value-per-effort) Particle cloze — `cloze:particle`.** Blank the **particle** in `example.jp` (`＿` where を/が/に/で/へ/は/と/も/の/か sits), learner picks the right one from the closed particle set. The single most-drilled grammar pain point, and a genuinely distinct skill from the shipped word-cloze. **Rides the shipped cloze card** — reuses its render + `deriveGrade({kind:"mc"})`; options are the fixed particle set (no distractor-building needed). Guard: the sentence has exactly one clearly-identifiable target particle (via the tokenizer, or a tiny content tag on the target token). Smallest of the four.
- [ ] **[R11] (Feature CC — brief-worthy, FLAGSHIP — Alex's idea) Sentence builder — `build:sentence`.** Scramble the **word + particle tokens** of `example.jp` into tiles; learner reassembles them in the correct order. Add 1–2 **distractor particle tiles** so it tests particle *choice*, not just ordering. It's the token-granularity version of the shipped `build` card (which assembles a *reading* from syllable tiles) — reuse that tile mechanic + `deriveGrade({kind:"typed"})`. Tests **word order + particle placement** = the core of production grammar. Needs the tokenizer keystone; guard `canBuildSentence`. Slots at the PRODUCED tier (rung 3). **This is the one to brief first.**
- [ ] **[R12] (Feature CC — rides R11) English → Japanese sentence production — `produce:sentence`.** Show only `example.en`, JA hidden; learner builds the JA sentence from tiles (R11's mechanic + a pool of plausible distractor words/particles). Because the reference sentence is hidden, it's **genuine production from meaning** — the deepest production short of free writing, yet ND-safe (tile assembly, not a blank page). Reuses R11's tokenizer + tile UI. Slots at top-of-PRODUCED / pre-SPOKEN — the "can you say it in Japanese?" bar, in tile form.
- [ ] **[R13] (Feature CC — ⚠️ needs new content data) Conjugation transform — `conjugate`.** Given a base/dictionary form + a target inflection (past ました · neg ません · plain ない · い-adj くない · past-adj かった · want たい), learner produces the conjugated form (tiles or typed → reuse `checkReading`). **Nothing tests grammatical *transformation* today**, and A1's whole grammar tail *is* conjugation. The one card with a real content cost: it needs **conjugation-pair data** (base → {past, neg, …}) = a schema/content addition (Curriculum + `contract.js`), unlike R10–R12 which reuse existing `example` data. Highest grammar-transformation value; ranked last only for that data dependency. *Route the data half to Curriculum CC once scoped.*

### Batch 6 — motivation model DECIDED (2026-07-10)

**Alex's philosophy call (2026-07-10):** asked "add more achievements?" + "get rid of streak/XP/freezes?", he chose **structural milestones only**. The line is **capability vs activity** — capability milestones (mark real skill gained) are the mission-aligned progress signal and get built; engagement rewards (streak/XP/freezes/day-counts) reward activity and are OUT. Codified in CLAUDE.md's anti-gamification rule the same day. This **confirms R17 / R18 / R30 as GO** (they were pending Alex's call).

- [ ] **[R35] (Feature CC — brief written; ⚠️ persist check-in) Milestones (capability achievements) + retire the engagement scoreboard. → `docs/shipped/BUILD-BRIEF-milestones.md` (Idea CC, 2026-07-10).** Two halves: **ADD** capability milestones — "can read all hiragana," "100 words mastered," "A1 complete," "all N5 kanji" — computed *from mastery state* (reuses `isLevelComplete` + `isMastered`; a data-driven milestone catalog + a pure `earnedMilestones(items,units)` selector; earned-once, never revoked; wire the dormant mascot `"achievement"` reaction, `DevPanel.jsx:15`). **REMOVE** the Today stat trio (streak/XP/freezes, `Today.jsx:259-263`) — the positive replacement for R17/R18/R30. Guardrail: milestones reward **capability, never activity** (no points/streaks/decay/FOMO). ⚠️ Removing streak/XP/freeze fields = persist/user-state change → Alex's check-in, migration-safe. Brief has the milestone catalog, phases (M.0 selector+tests first), and DoD.

See CLAUDE.md → "Three CC lanes."

**Alex: "Reset works."** The one item in the 100-commit release that no automated environment could reach is confirmed working against live Supabase. Closed.

**Original entry, kept for the record:**

### DEFERRED BY ALEX — reset/sync verification (2026-09-02)

**Shipped to prod unverified, knowingly.** `main` `9a3311b5` was pushed with the reset/sync fix never exercised against a live Supabase. Alex was told the risk twice and chose to ship and revisit — recorded so the decision is traceable and the item is not lost.

- **What is unverified:** sign in -> load progress -> Settings -> Reset everything -> wait for "Progress reset — saved to your account" -> force-close -> reopen (must still be reset). Then the RACE: repeat WITHOUT waiting for the toast, force-close within a second, reopen.
- **Stop condition:** if the toast ever reads "saved on this device" while signed in, the account is not attached — a different and worse bug.
- **Why no automated test can cover it:** `App.jsx:32` sets `AUTH_ENABLED = supabase configured && !IS_WEBDRIVER`. Under Playwright it is false, so auth and onboarding never render; spoofing `navigator.webdriver` flips it true and the run lands on the login wall instead. **The same flag gates audio playback**, so no single automated run can have both app access and audio. Only a real signed-in device closes this.
- **Blast radius if wrong:** real user progress — the one item among the 100 merged commits that touches persisted learner state.

### A1 curriculum QA pass (2026-06-30) — U7–15, 17–21 read item-by-item

**Verdict: A1 is in good shape — no hard bugs.** No crashes, no duplicate item ids, no duplicate vocab fronts, no validator/lint failures. Romaji all normalizable; particle readings correct (は=wa, を=wo, へ=e). Every "duplicate meaning" is an *intentional* kana-word-vs-kanji pair (いち↔一, たべます↔食) — fronts differ so mastery tracks independently; not a defect. Number/time/family/food/place vocab all accurate; humble/honorific family split handled well; verb kanji use dictionary-form readings with matching ます-form examples; 知る→知っています correct. Findings below are **naturalness/pedagogy items for the batched native review** (the gate that already governs kanji+grammar) — none block.

- [ ] **P2 — Forward kanji references in kanji-unit examples (confirmed + enumerated; was flagged generically).** A kanji appears in an example before its own teaching unit: **U13** 電→`電車で行きます` (車 is U18, 行 is U17); **U13** 気→`元気ですか` (元 is U18); **U14** 友→`友だちが来ます` (来 is U17); **U14** 先→`先生に聞きます` (聞 is U17); **U14** 手→`手を見ます` (見 is U17); **U14** 足→`足が長いです` (長 is U18). Learner meets the glyph as "unknown kanji" mid-example. **Fix (Curriculum CC, native-review batch):** either write these examples in kana until the kanji is introduced, or reorder the kanji units to the category scheme (⚠️ id-churn resets that kanji's mastery — do it in the same deliberate pass, pre-users).
- [ ] **P2 — U18 adjective-kanji reading inconsistency.** 大 is taught reading **`dai`** and 小 **`shō`** (on-readings), but their examples `大きい`/`小さい` — and *every* sibling adjective kanji in the unit (高`takai`, 安`yasui`, 新`atarashii`, 古`furui`, 多`ōi`, 少`sukunai`, 長`nagai`, 白`shiroi`) — use **kun** readings that match the example word. So for 大/小 the shown reading doesn't match the reading in the example sentence (confusing at recognition time). **Fix (Curriculum CC, native-review):** give 大/小 the kun reading (おお…/ちい…) for consistency, or split the on/kun explicitly in the hint. Additive if only the `reading`/`hint` change; id-safe.
- [ ] **P3 — U14L2 `生` glossed "student".** 生 in isolation means life/birth/raw; "student" is only the 学生/先生 *suffix* sense. As a recognition gloss it mis-teaches 生 (e.g. 生きる, 誕生). **Fix (Curriculum CC, native-review):** gloss as "life / birth" with the student sense in the hint, or "(せい) student; life". Low risk (recognition only).
- [ ] **P3 — U10L5 `きれい` grouped with い-adjectives.** It sits among ちかい/とおい/おおきい… (all true い-adjectives) but is grammatically a **な-adjective**; risk the learner over-generalizes to ✗`きれくない`. Taught as vocab so nothing breaks today — **flag for when U21's adjective-conjugation lessons are cross-checked** (make sure な-adjectives aren't swept into the い-conjugation drill). (Curriculum CC.)
- [ ] **P4 — minor glosses (native-review polish, batch them):** U8L3 `おじいさん`/`おばあさん` glossed "old man/old woman" reads oddly inside the *honorific-family* lesson (siblings are "(someone's) grandfather/grandmother"); U7L5 `ひる` "noon" is really midday/daytime; U12L1 `そらはあおです` is slightly less natural than `あおいです` (and U12L2 gives the あおい version anyway). None block. (Curriculum CC.)
- [x] **P3 — Docs: README curriculum counts were stale — FIXED 2026-06-30 (QA CC).** README said **21 units · 82 lessons · 604 items**; now reads **A1 content-complete · 21 units · 93 lessons · 729 items**. Also corrected the kanji-unit list (kanji = Units 11, 13–15, 17–18; grammar = 19–21, previously mislabeled as kanji), added the core-A1-grammar bullet, and moved "particles & grammar" out of "Not yet built" (it's authored; only the native review remains). Doc-only edit, no code/content touched.

- [ ] **P1 — `src/components/games/RecallCard.jsx` is uncommitted dead code that violates the no-self-grading principle.** (Feature CC / Alex to decide.) It's untracked, imported nowhere, and **not** a `LIVE_CARD_KINDS` entry (kinds are teach/choice/type:meaning/build/trace — note `dominantMode:"recall"` in units is the *pedagogical mode*, unrelated). Worse, it renders **user-tapped Again/Hard/Good/Easy grade buttons** — the exact self-grading the engine rejects (Phase 0: "app-judged cards, computed FSRS grade from correctness+speed, **no self-grading**"). Its own comment falsely claims it's "Fully wired." **Action:** delete it, or if a manual-recall card is genuinely wanted, spec it as a real engine change (draft PR, add to `LIVE_CARD_KINDS` + coverage fixture) — but reconcile it with the no-self-grading rule first. Not QA's to build.
- [ ] **P3 — `ja-u16l6` density advisory** (3 word cards vs 5–8). Yōon tail lesson; finite set so may be acceptable. Curriculum CC: either thicken with review items or confirm-and-waive. Non-blocking.

## Future / come back later (concepts & growth — not yet scheduled)


- **🇺🇸 THE APP IS FOR THE AMERICAN MARKET RIGHT NOW — Alex, 2026-09-13.** *"We can do this last, this app for the american market rn."* Said about **source-language support** (onboarding asking what language you speak, then running the app in it), which is now scheduled **last**.
  - **What that means in practice:** the learner speaks English. Every gloss, hint, example and accepted answer stays in English, and that is correct rather than a gap. The app teaches ja / fr / es / de / no / pt **to English speakers**.
  - **It settles three open threads at once, all parked together:** source-language support, the three English companions (American/British/Australian), and British-vs-American English. **All three only matter once English is a TAUGHT language**, and English cannot be taught to someone who already speaks it. They unpark together, in that order, or not at all.
  - **The measured reason it is last, and it is the real one:** teaching in a new source language means translating **75,688 strings / 2.2 million characters — about 1,800 pages — per language the learner might speak** (every `meaning`, `accept[]`, `hint`, `example.en`, `drill.en` and lesson `canDo` across 13,408 items). The app's own buttons and screens are only **~228 phrases** by comparison. It is a 330× gap between the two halves of "translate the app", and the big half does not scale the way audio does — there is no equivalent of one paid TTS run.
  - ⚠️ **The one thing that gets more expensive with delay:** it changes the shape of every card — an item stops having one `meaning` and starts having one per source language. That is a contract change across all 13,408 items, and it is far cheaper before real users than after. Parking the *work* is right; the *schema* question is worth settling before launch rather than after.
Parking for ideas and growth tasks we've named but aren't building yet. Per the standing rule (#9 above), everything we discuss lands here so it's not lost. Promote items into a real phase when they're ready to build.

Each should run on the existing item/SRS data (a game session can feed grades back into FSRS so playing = reviewing). Decide whether they're a separate tab or woven into the session. Its own sprint; scope when picked up.
- **Standard language pathway — see `BUILD-BRIEF-language-blueprint.md` (Alex, 2026-08-02): "we need a standard so creating other languages is easy and I can mass-do it with multiple CC running."** Correct read — there was no written standard, only French's de-facto one. **Japanese is the model** (Alex's call 2026-08-02 — "follows the structure of ja since that one is basically done right"). The brief extracts ja's actual shape: **three interleaved strands per CEFR band** — script/sound (taught in chunks that are immediately used for real words: ja U1 = 25 kana + 29 vocab), thematic vocab, and grammar-as-function-word-vocab (copula → verbs & particles → past tense & agreement) — plus a **coverage pass** closing each band. **A Latin-script language is the identical template with the script strand collapsed to one unit**; that's the only difference. Density = the mature ja shape, **4 lessons × 6 cards = 24 cards/unit** (u22 onward; ja's 47–55-card U1–U10 are pre-lint drift, explicitly not the model — fr independently landed at 21, same target). Also flagged: ja's `order`/`stage` interleave inconsistently (pre-a1 reappears at u16, a1 at u53–68 and u82–87) — a new language keeps `order` monotonic within `stage`. Operational half is `RUNBOOK-new-language.md` (§0 = the one line Alex types; §7 = the stuck-table that makes it no-questions-asked). B1/B2 spine unspecified until ja gets there. **Prerequisites: (a)(b)(c) ✓ DONE 2026-08-02, branch `feat/language-prereqs` (commit `aefa82f`) — draft, awaiting Alex's merge.** Full gate green (validate, lint, 189 unit tests, audit, build, Playwright dev 27 + preview 25). Shipped with it: **`isLive` now requires *playable* content** — a scaffolded language of locked stubs was flipping live with nothing learnable, which `tests/unit/prune-languages.test.mjs` caught because it would also have defeated the stale-save migration in `useStore`. **(d) downgraded — not a blocker** (see below). The four as originally filed: (a) **word-front uniqueness is global across languages** — `contract.js` + `lint.js` key the map on `front` with no lang, so es `no` + it `no` is a hard CI failure (verified by running `validateContent` directly); it fails at *merge* time, so parallel sessions are each green alone and red together; (b) `src/data/index.js` is a merge-conflict funnel (one import + one array entry per unit in a single shared file) → generate a per-language barrel instead (**not** `import.meta.glob` — Vite-only, and the `node --test` unit tests import that file); (c) no `scaffold:lang` script, so a new language starts by hand-copying an existing one; (d) ~~the `reading` contract blocks 5 languages outright~~ — **CORRECTED 2026-08-02 after testing both paths: nothing is blocked.** Readings are authored as the *ASCII fold* (the French convention: `s'il vous plaît` → `silvousplait`), so Norwegian authors `øl` → `ol` and validates clean; and a learner typing the real word is still accepted because `checkReading` matches `raw === item.front` before folding. The genuine defect is narrower and already live: **`reading` is *displayed* as a pronunciation guide** while being an ASCII typing key — filed as a Feature CC item above. The lossy-fold issue for tonal languages (`ma má mà mả mã mạ` → all `ma`) is real but deferred until a tonal language is scheduled. **Crews are not blocked by (d).**
- **AI tiers = the monetization model (Alex, 2026-08-02) — not scoped yet; revisit when ja hits B2.** The plan in Alex's words: AI access starts **limited** for everyone; as a learner progresses, the app **requires** conversation with the AI so they actually practise speaking. **Free** users get that progression-gated practice only. **Paid** users get open-ended AI — "ask it to translate a song, ask about words, just have conversations" — i.e. the tutor as a general tool, not only a drill partner. **Timing:** attack this once **Japanese is finished through B2**; ja sets the standard and the other languages copy it *(unless French finishes first — then fr sets it)*. Nothing to build now; this is the shape to design against. Infrastructure already in place: the Haruki tab (Phase 6.5, PR #29) is a live ElevenLabs Conversational Agent, and `inventoryFor({lang, maxLevel, maxRung})` already scopes what the tutor may see by CEFR + rung — that selector is the natural lever for "AI unlocks as you climb."
  - **Open questions to settle when we attack it** (log only, no decision yet): (1) **Cost floor** — conversational minutes bill per minute, so "limited" needs a real unit (minutes/day? turns/session?) before pricing means anything. (2) **Required-conversation vs. the anti-burnout spine** — a *required* AI turn that a learner can't complete (mic anxiety, no quiet room, ND load) becomes a hard blocker on the ladder; needs a non-speaking fallback path (text chat already exists in the unified Haruki chat) so the requirement gates *practice*, not *progress*. (3) **Free-tier honesty** — what a free user is promised up front, so the paywall reads as "more tool," never as "we took your tutor away." (4) Payments/entitlements = new dependency + backend scope (Phase 6 territory), its own brief.
- **Sign language — PARKED, and it gets its OWN STRUCTURE (Alex, 2026-09-03).** Decided after scoping it: *"we'll add it later, it'll have its own structure."* Not a catalog entry, not the language blueprint, not a `LANGUAGES[]` row — a second modality alongside the existing one. Do not try to fit it into `src/data/<lang>/` conventions when it comes.
  - **Why it cannot reuse the structure.** Two load-bearing assumptions break. (1) **There is no typeable `front`.** A sign is handshape + location + movement + palm orientation + non-manual markers; the written stand-ins are all wrong for teaching — *gloss* (`MOTHER`, `GO-TO`) is an English label for a sign, so teaching gloss teaches English, and HamNoSys/SignWriting are real notation nobody reads and no keyboard types. `front` has to be **video**, which kills every card that types or manipulates a string: `type:meaning`, `type:produce`, `build`, `cloze:choice`, `sentence:build`. (2) **Audio is the perception channel** — `listen:choice`, `listen:type` and `speak` all die with it. Add that ASL grammar is topic-comment with spatial agreement and classifiers, carried in **simultaneous non-manual markers** rather than word order, so the blueprint's "grammar as function-word vocab" has nothing to attach to.
  - **"Sign language" is not one language.** ASL · BSL · LSF · Auslan are unrelated — BSL and ASL are not mutually intelligible (ASL descends from LSF). Whatever the structure is, it is per-language like everything else.
  - **What the engine already gives for free:** media is a **manifest of item ids** (`AUDIO_IDS.has(item.id)` → `public/audio/<id>.mp3`), so a parallel `VIDEO_IDS` → `public/video/<id>.mp4` with `hasVideo()` is small, and the routing gates already branch on `hasAudio`. FSRS, the rungs, the daily loop and milestones are modality-agnostic and need nothing.
  - **The wall is production grading.** Typing and STT both die. Self-assessment is honest but gives FSRS a self-reported grade (a real weakening of the signal); in-browser hand/pose tracking handles isolated handshapes and is an open research problem for real signing with coarticulation and non-manuals — **a confidently wrong grade is worse than no grade**; human review does not scale. Settle this before authoring anything.
  - **The strategic fact, and the reason it is parked behind de/no/pt:** every other language scales through TTS — one paid `generate:audio` run and the band is voiced. **There is no TTS for sign.** Every clip is human-produced or licensed, forever, thousands per band. It is the first language whose content cost does not fall with scale. It also requires **Deaf signers producing the content** — not a nice-to-have; a hearing-built ASL course is a known failure mode and would be judged as one.
  - **The first slice, when it is picked up: FINGERSPELLING, on its own.** The manual alphabet is a closed set of 26 handshapes, structurally identical to kana — one glyph, one meaning, no grammar — so `front` stays typeable (the letter) and recognition/production work today's way. **Receptive fingerspelling** (reading a fingerspelled word at speed) is the genuinely hard and useful skill, and it is `listen:choice` with video swapped for audio. **~30–100 clips, not thousands.** It proves the video manifest, the card kinds and the Deaf-consultant relationship before anyone commits to a curriculum.

Alex's profile predates the picker and carries the retired ja→es→fr cascade seeding, so whatever it recorded is permanent.
  - ⚠️ **Do not "fix" this by pruning harder.** If a learner has real progress in a language, listing it as started is correct — and the prune already burned itself once by inferring intent from content (2026-07-31, erosive: it re-fired on every boot and deleted re-added languages). The honest fix is a **"stop learning this"** action: removes it from `profile.languages`, keeps its item progress untouched so re-adding restores it, and refuses to remove the last one. Small, and it is the missing half of `startLanguage`.
- [ ] **(Feature CC) The Ladder needs a sounds/accents section of its own (Alex, 2026-09-03).** *"Accents should have their own section, not be under Word bank — accents and whatever else, then Word bank, then phrases if we implement them."* Right: the Ladder already has per-content-type sections (`YoonSection`, `KanjiSection`) for exactly this reason, and the fr sounds unit (`fr-u27` lessons 1–2: é è ê ç ô û œ, then eau/au/ai/oi/ui/gn/ill) currently dissolves into the general Word bank where it reads as vocabulary rather than as a sound system. Add a `SoundsSection` on the same pattern, ordered **sounds → word bank → phrases**. Latin-script languages only; ja's equivalent is the kana grid it already has. **Phrases has no data model yet** — a phrase is not a vocab item; that is its own question, not a section to add speculatively.

Listing it as a **planned** row is harmless and makes the intent visible; what must not happen is a crew treating that row as a normal scaffold target. If it goes in, the entry needs a comment saying so, and ✌️ is the right mark — sign languages have no country flag, and ASL/BSL/LSF/Auslan are unrelated languages that would each need their own row anyway.

An American learner never meets an English course, so the three voices have nobody to be shown to yet. **Do not build.** Keep the costing below; it is measured and will still be true when this comes back. The one piece worth taking early is the *voice axis itself* (a language having more than one voice at all), and it is wanted first by **pt-BR vs pt-PT**, not by English.

Supersedes the GB/US entry below.** *"That does mean English will have 3x audios."* Correct, and the number is worth seeing before committing: the CURRENT corpus is **10,200 clips / 180 MB** for all three languages combined (ja 5,012 · fr 3,104 · es 2,084, ~18 KB each). An English track sized like French, voiced three ways, is **~9,300 clips / ~165 MB — one language nearly doubling the app's entire audio payload**, plus three ElevenLabs ConvAI agents for Alex to create and a paid generation run ~3× larger than any so far. Audio is fetched on demand, not precached (the SW precache is ~5 MB), so this is deploy size and bandwidth rather than install size.
  - ✅ **SETTLED (Alex, 2026-09-04): VOICE, not content.** *"The whole language would be taught in that voice while the others are hidden."* One shared corpus, three audio sets, the learner picks one at start and never sees the others. That is the bounded version — it is audio + companion wiring, **not** three parallel corpora with a variant axis through every card.
  - **What that makes the real cost:** 3× audio on the SERVER (~165 MB for an English-sized track), but **1× per learner** — clips are fetched on demand, so a learner only ever pulls their own variant. Deploy weight and one paid generation run, not a per-learner download tax.

Cheap (the `accept[]` machinery already exists) but it must be decided per item at authoring time, not discovered later. Spanish and Portuguese variants do not have this problem, which is another reason to build the mechanism on **pt-BR/pt-PT first** and let English inherit it.

Building the variant machinery English-first means building it for the one language that currently cannot launch.
  - **So build it for VARIANTS generally, not for English.** The same mechanism is wanted sooner and by languages that can ship: **pt-BR vs pt-PT** (a wider split than en-US/en-GB, and Portuguese is one of the three scaffolds about to get crews), **es Spain vs Latin America**, fr France vs Québec. Doing it once generally is far cheaper than doing it English-shaped and retrofitting.
  - **Engine surface it touches:** `/audio/<lang>/<id>.mp3` plus a flat `AUDIO_IDS` set (`hasAudio` keys on the id alone) — a variant has to enter the path and the manifest; `server/companions.js` is keyed by language and would key on language+variant; the learner's pick becomes a persisted, synced setting; and `generate-audio.mjs` gains a variant loop. None of it is hard; all of it is cheaper designed once.

Superseded by the entry above and parked with it.
- [ ] **(Product, Alex 2026-09-03) British vs American English — and the blocker is not the variants.** Alex: *"for English I'm thinking we add British and American, unless you think that's dumb."* Not dumb, but **English of any kind is blocked by something else**: the app has no source-language concept. Every `meaning`, `accept` and `example.en` IS English, so an English track asks the learner to translate English into English (`LANGUAGES.md` documents this). Two English rows would be two blocked tracks. **The variant idea is worth keeping without the tracks** — GB/US differences are a *note on an item*, not a curriculum, which is the same shape as the next entry.
- [ ] **(Product, Alex 2026-09-03) Old English as post-answer fun facts — the best-shaped of these ideas.** Alex: *"not for cards, but like fun facts — when on a card and you answer, it can say in olde English it's said like this."* This fits the app's spine (deep understanding over memorisation) and costs the engine almost nothing: an optional `note` on an item, surfaced in the feedback state that already exists after an answer. It generalises past Old English to etymology, GB/US variants, false friends, and register — one field, many uses. **The cost is content, as always**: ~10,000 notes if it is required, so it must be OPTIONAL and authored opportunistically, shown only when present. Do not gate mastery on it and do not let it become a per-item authoring obligation.
